why: A Product Owner is judged less on the backlog than on direction: can the team, the managers and the customers see where the product is going, why, and roughly when? Roadmaps, stakeholder work and honest forecasts are where most PO interviews and most PO conflicts happen.
outcome: You can write a product vision and a Product Goal, build an outcome roadmap (now, next, later), map and align stakeholders, say no with data, play your part in the Scrum events, forecast a release as a range, and measure value with Evidence-Based Management.

lessons.title: Product vision and strategy
text: The product vision describes the change the product brings to its users, several years out: who it is for, which problem it removes and why it will win. It is not a feature list. A good vision stays stable while the features change many times, and it lets anyone on the team decide whether an idea belongs in the product.

A classic way to write it is Geoffrey Moore’s positioning statement from Crossing the Chasm: for (target customer) who (need), the (product) is a (category) that (key benefit); unlike (main alternative), our product (difference). Positioning forces two choices that teams avoid: who the product is not for, and what it will not try to beat competitors on.

The product strategy is the plan to move toward the vision: which customer segment first, which problem first, how the product makes money and what makes it hard to copy. Roman Pichler’s Product Vision Board puts the vision, target group, needs, product and business goals on one page; it is a convenient format for a workshop with managers.

The 2020 Scrum Guide adds the Product Goal: the future state of the product that the Scrum Team plans against, the commitment of the Product Backlog. The Scrum Team works on one Product Goal at a time and fulfils it or abandons it before taking the next. In practice it is a step toward the vision that fits in a few months, for example “Small shops can run their payroll without an accountant by June”.

In interviews, expect “What is the vision of the product you worked on?” Answer in one sentence for the vision, one for the current Product Goal, and one number that shows progress. Candidates who answer with a list of features show they have managed a backlog, not a product.
points: Vision: the long-term change for users; stable for years.
Positioning statement: target customer, need, category, key benefit, alternative, difference.
Product strategy: which segment, which problem, which business model first.
Product Goal (Scrum Guide 2020): the next measurable step toward the vision, one at a time.
Test every big idea against the vision before it enters the backlog.

example.code:
Vision
  Every small shop runs its people admin in ten minutes a month.

Positioning statement
  For owners of shops with 1 to 20 staff
  who lose an evening a week on payroll and leave requests,
  ShopTeam is an HR app
  that pays staff and files payroll declarations in a few clicks.
  Unlike generic accounting software,
  it is built for shift work and needs no accountant.

Product Goal (next 4 months)
  Shops with up to 20 staff run payroll without an accountant.
  Measured by: 60 % of active shops run payroll alone by June.
example.note: Three levels: the vision rarely changes, the positioning chooses who it is for, the Product Goal is the next measurable step.

lessons.title: Roadmaps: features or outcomes, now, next, later
text: A roadmap is a statement of intent: the problems the team will work on, in which order and why. It is not a release plan with dates per feature. A feature roadmap (a Gantt chart of “SSO in March, dashboard in April”) promises outputs months ahead, when the team knows least, and turns every change of plan into a broken promise.

An outcome roadmap lists the results to reach (“cut checkout drop-off from 70 % to 60 %”) and the problems to solve, grouped by themes. Features appear only as current ideas under an outcome, and they can be replaced by better ones. Stakeholders see what the product will achieve; the team keeps the freedom to find the best solution.

The now / next / later format, made popular by Janna Bastow of ProdPad, replaces dates with horizons of growing uncertainty. Now: what the team is working on, detailed and committed. Next: what comes after, shaped but open to change. Later: problems worth solving, deliberately vague. Items move left as evidence comes in, and items in Later can disappear without anyone losing face.

Themes group the work around a goal or a customer problem (“Onboarding”, “Trust and compliance”, “Mobile shift workers”). They make the roadmap readable for managers, help balance the investment between new value, improvements and technical work, and keep the conversation on why rather than on which button.

Keep one roadmap and several views: a detailed one for the team, a theme-level one for management, a public one with no dates for customers. Review it at least once a quarter and after any big learning. A roadmap that never changes is either not used or not honest.
points: Feature roadmap: outputs with dates. Outcome roadmap: results to reach, with features as ideas.
Now / next / later: horizons of growing uncertainty instead of dates.
Themes group work by goal or customer problem.
Every item says why: the outcome, the evidence, the metric.
Same roadmap, different views for team, management and customers.

example.code:
NOW (committed, this quarter)
  Theme: Payroll without an accountant
    Outcome: 60 % of shops run payroll alone (today 35 %)
    Ideas: guided first payroll, automatic declarations

NEXT (shaped, open to change)
  Theme: Fewer support tickets
    Outcome: payroll tickets per 100 shops from 18 to 10
    Ideas: error checks before submit, in-app help

LATER (problems worth solving)
  Theme: Multi-site shops
    Problem: owners with 2+ shops copy data by hand
  Theme: Mobile shift workers
    Problem: staff cannot swap shifts without calling
example.note: No dates per feature: each horizon carries outcomes and problems, and the ideas under them can change.

lessons.title: Stakeholder mapping and alignment
text: Stakeholders are everyone who affects the product or is affected by it: users, buyers, sales, support, marketing, finance, legal, security, the operations team, senior management. The Product Owner does not have to please all of them; the PO has to know them, understand what each one needs and make trade-offs that are visible.

The power / interest grid (often credited to Mendelow) sorts stakeholders on two axes. High power and high interest: manage closely, involve them in decisions. High power, low interest: keep satisfied, short updates, no surprises. Low power, high interest: keep informed, they are often power users and good sources of feedback. Low power, low interest: monitor, with general communication.

Draw the map at the start of a product or a big initiative and redraw it when people change: a new sales director can move from “keep satisfied” to “manage closely” in a week. Note for each person what success means to them, their main worry and how they like to be informed. A legal team that wants written answers will not be won over in a hallway chat.

Alignment comes from rhythm more than from big meetings. The Sprint Review is the main place where stakeholders see the Increment and adjust the Product Backlog. Add a monthly or quarterly roadmap review with key stakeholders, short one-to-ones with the most powerful ones, and a written update that anyone can read. Decisions and their reasons go in writing.

What goes wrong in real jobs: the PO meets only the loudest stakeholder; requests arrive by e-mail to developers and bypass the Product Backlog; two directors give opposite priorities and the PO tries to satisfy both. The fix is the same each time: one Product Backlog, one person who orders it, and open trade-offs in front of the people who disagree.
points: Power / interest grid: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor.
Note for each stakeholder: their success, their worry, their preferred channel.
Sprint Review plus a regular roadmap review keep people aligned.
All requests go into the one Product Backlog, not straight to developers.
Write decisions and their reasons down.

example.code:
LOW INTEREST            HIGH INTEREST
HIGH POWER   Keep satisfied            Manage closely
             - CFO (monthly figures)    - Head of Sales
             - Legal (written review)   - COO, product sponsor
LOW POWER    Monitor                    Keep informed
             - Facilities               - Support team leads
             - Other product teams      - 12 pilot shops
example.note: Each quadrant gets its own strategy and channel; the map is redrawn when people or priorities change.

lessons.title: Saying no and negotiating scope
text: Every yes is a no to something else: the team has a fixed capacity, so a new item pushes another one down the Product Backlog. The cost of yes is the delay of everything below it, the context switching, and the maintenance of a feature forever. Saying no is part of the job; the 2020 Scrum Guide says that for Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions.

Say no to the solution, not to the person. Start by understanding the need behind the request: “What problem would this solve, for whom, and what happens if we do nothing?” Often the real need is smaller than the request, or already covered by an item on the roadmap.

Bring data to the conversation: how many customers have the problem, revenue at stake, support tickets, usage of a similar feature, effort estimate. A simple score such as RICE (reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort) or the cost of delay turns a fight between opinions into a comparison everyone can see.

Negotiate scope rather than give a flat refusal: a smaller first version, a workaround, a test before the build, a later horizon on the roadmap. When time and people are fixed, scope is the variable. Make the trade-off explicit: “We can do it this quarter if we move the invoice export to next; which one matters more to you?”

Close the loop. Tell the requester what you decided and why, and where the request now sits. A no with reasons keeps trust; a silent no or a vague “maybe later” destroys it. In interviews, a story where you said no to a senior stakeholder with data, offered an alternative and kept the relationship is one of the strongest a PO can tell.
points: Every yes is a no to something else: show what moves down.
Ask for the problem behind the request before discussing the solution.
Use data and a visible score (RICE, cost of delay).
Fixed time and people: negotiate the scope.
Always tell the requester the decision and the reason.

example.code:
Request (Head of Sales): "Add a custom PDF quote builder for the Big Retail deal."

1. Need:     Big Retail wants branded quotes; 1 prospect asked, 0 customers.
2. Cost:     about 3 sprints; pushes "automatic declarations" (Product Goal) by 6 weeks.
3. Data:     automatic declarations affects 2,400 active shops.
4. Options:  a) logo + colours on the existing quote (2 days)
             b) full builder in NEXT if 5+ prospects ask
5. Decision: option a) now; b) added to NEXT with a trigger.
6. Told:     Head of Sales + sales channel, with the reasons, same day.
example.note: The need is met in a smaller form, the trade-off is written down, and the request has a clear place and trigger.

lessons.title: The Product Owner in the Scrum events
text: The 2020 Scrum Guide defines three accountabilities in a Scrum Team: the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the Developers. The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team, and for effective Product Backlog management: developing and communicating the Product Goal, creating and communicating Product Backlog items, ordering them, and making sure the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood. The PO can delegate this work but remains accountable. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee.

Sprint Planning: the PO comes with the Product Backlog ordered and explains how the most important items relate to the Product Goal. The whole Scrum Team crafts the Sprint Goal. The Developers decide how much they can take into the Sprint and how they will do the work; the PO does not assign tasks or push extra items in. Sprint Planning is time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, shorter for shorter Sprints.

Product Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not a Scrum event in the 2020 guide: items are broken down and given more detail, order and size. The Developers who will do the work are responsible for the sizing; the PO brings the why, the acceptance criteria and the answers. The Daily Scrum belongs to the Developers; the PO attends only if also working on Sprint Backlog items, or listens without steering.

Sprint Review: the Scrum Team presents the results of its work to key stakeholders and they discuss progress toward the Product Goal. It is a working session, not a demo for applause: the PO invites the right people, discusses what changed in the market, and the Product Backlog may be adjusted. Time-box: four hours at most for a one-month Sprint. In the Sprint Retrospective, the PO takes part as a team member.

Working with the Scrum Master and the Developers: the Scrum Master helps the PO with techniques for the Product Goal and backlog management and with stakeholder collaboration; the Developers own the Sprint Backlog and the quality (Definition of Done). Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel a Sprint, if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Interviewers check these boundaries: a PO who “assigns stories to developers” or “approves estimates” fails the question.
points: Three accountabilities: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers.
PO: maximizes value, owns the Product Goal and the order of the Product Backlog; one person.
Developers decide how much they pull into the Sprint and how they do it.
Refinement is an ongoing activity; Developers size the items.
Sprint Review: a working session with stakeholders; only the PO can cancel a Sprint.

example.code:
Event / activity     The PO brings                        The PO does not
Sprint Planning      ordered backlog, link to Product Goal   choose how much the Developers take
Daily Scrum          (optional, as a listener)            run it or ask for status reports
Refinement           why, acceptance criteria, answers    impose estimates
Sprint Review        stakeholders, market news, priorities  give a slide show with no discussion
Retrospective        their view as a team member          use it to judge the Developers
example.note: The PO decides what and why; the Developers decide how and how much.

lessons.title: Release planning and forecasting with velocity
text: Velocity is the amount of work, usually in story points, that a team finishes per Sprint according to the Definition of Done. It is a planning aid for that team only: it cannot be compared between teams, and it stops being useful the moment it becomes a target, because points then inflate.

The basic forecast: sprints needed = remaining points ÷ average velocity, rounded up, since a team does not finish a release in part of a Sprint. With 240 points left and an average velocity of 34, 240 ÷ 34 = 7.06, so 8 Sprints. In Excel: =ROUNDUP(B2/C2,0). With two-week Sprints, that is 16 weeks.

A single number hides the uncertainty. Use a range from the team’s recent lowest and highest velocity: with 28 to 42 points per Sprint, the same 240 points need 6 to 9 Sprints. Say “between 6 and 9 Sprints, most likely 8” rather than a date. Monte Carlo forecasts built from past throughput (items finished per week) give the same kind of answer with probabilities, such as “85 % chance by week 18”.

The backlog is not fixed either: new items arrive and items grow during refinement. Track scope with a release burn-up chart, which shows the work done and the total scope as two lines; when the scope line keeps rising, the release date moves even if the team works well. Update the forecast every Sprint and tell stakeholders when it moves.

Fixed date or fixed scope? When the date cannot move (a legal deadline, a trade fair), order the backlog so the most valuable items come first and accept that the scope will flex. When the scope cannot move, the date is the output of the forecast. Adding people late rarely helps: new people need onboarding and coordination grows, as Brooks’s law says. Give ranges, not promises.
points: Velocity: done work per Sprint, for one team’s planning only; never a target.
Sprints needed = ROUNDUP(remaining points ÷ average velocity).
Forecast as a range from the lowest and highest recent velocity.
Release burn-up: done work and total scope; growing scope moves the date.
Fixed date means flexible scope; give ranges, not promises.

example.code:
Remaining points (B2): 240
Average velocity (C2): 34      Lowest (D2): 28      Highest (E2): 42
Sprint length in weeks (F2): 2

Sprints needed       =ROUNDUP(B2/C2,0)        -> 8
Optimistic           =ROUNDUP(B2/E2,0)        -> 6
Pessimistic          =ROUNDUP(B2/D2,0)        -> 9
Weeks to release     =ROUNDUP(B2/C2,0)*F2     -> 16
Range                =ROUNDUP(B2/E2,0)&" to "&ROUNDUP(B2/D2,0)&" sprints"  -> 6 to 9 sprints
example.note: The highest velocity gives the optimistic end of the range, the lowest the pessimistic end.

lessons.title: Evidence-Based Management and measuring value
text: Evidence-Based Management (EBM) is a framework published by Scrum.org to measure value and improve the ability to deliver it, using evidence rather than opinion. It replaces output measures (stories done, points, features shipped) with measures of what customers and the organization actually get.

EBM looks at four Key Value Areas. Current Value: the value the product delivers today (customer or user satisfaction, usage, revenue per employee). Unrealized Value: the value still possible (the gap between what customers want and what they get, market share not yet won). Time to Market: how fast the organization can deliver and learn (lead time, release frequency, time to learn from an experiment). Ability to Innovate: how well it can deliver new capabilities (share of time spent on new value rather than maintenance and defects, technical debt).

EBM sets goals at three levels: a Strategic Goal (ambitious and far, like a vision), Intermediate Goals (milestones on the way) and Immediate Tactical Goals (what the team aims at now, close to a Sprint Goal). Teams run small experiments toward the next goal, inspect the Key Value Measures and adapt.

Reading the areas together prevents bad decisions. High Current Value and low Ability to Innovate means a product living on past work, with growing technical debt. High Unrealized Value and a long Time to Market means opportunities that the organization is too slow to catch. A PO who only reports revenue sees the first problem too late.

Pick a few measures per area, measure them regularly and show the trend at the Sprint Review or the roadmap review. Vanity metrics (page views, number of features) feel good and change no decision; a good measure is tied to an outcome on the roadmap and tells you whether to continue, change or stop.
points: EBM (Scrum.org): measure value with evidence, not output.
Four Key Value Areas: Current Value, Unrealized Value, Time to Market, Ability to Innovate.
Goals: Strategic Goal, Intermediate Goals, Immediate Tactical Goals.
Read the four areas together to see the trade-offs.
Avoid vanity metrics: each measure supports a decision.

example.code:
Key Value Area        Example measure                          Now     Trend
Current Value         shops running payroll alone              35 %    up
                      customer satisfaction (survey, /10)      7.2     flat
Unrealized Value      shops still using an accountant          65 %    down
Time to Market        lead time, idea to production (days)     41      down
                      releases per month                       2       up
Ability to Innovate   time on new features vs fixes            45 %    down
                      open defects                             120     up
example.note: Value grows, but the share of time on new features falls and defects rise: technical debt is building up.

lessons.title: PSPO I and the Product Owner career
text: Professional Scrum Product Owner I (PSPO I) is Scrum.org’s first Product Owner certification. The assessment is online, multiple choice and timed (at the time of writing, 80 questions in 60 minutes with an 85 % pass mark; check Scrum.org before booking), it needs no course, and the certification does not expire. It covers the Scrum Guide from the Product Owner’s point of view, value and Product Backlog management, product vision and strategy, stakeholders, forecasting and release planning, and Evidence-Based Management.

The questions test the exact wording of the Scrum Guide and its spirit: who is accountable for what, what is an event or an activity, what the PO decides alone and what the Developers decide. Prepare with the Scrum Guide (2020 version) read several times, the EBM Guide, and the open practice assessment on Scrum.org. Scrum Alliance’s CSPO is the other common certificate; it is earned by attending a course with a Scrum Alliance trainer.

Product Owner and Product Manager overlap a lot and companies use the titles differently. Often the Product Manager looks outward and further ahead (market, pricing, strategy, several teams), while the Product Owner works closely with one or two Scrum Teams on the backlog and delivery. In other companies one person does both. Read the job description, not the title.

PO interviews mix four kinds of questions: product sense (“How would you improve this app?”), prioritisation (“Ten requests, capacity for three: what do you do?”), stakeholders (“Tell me about a time you said no”) and delivery (“The CEO wants a date”). Prepare three or four STAR stories with numbers: the situation, your action, the outcome measured.

Many POs come from business analysis, support, development, data or the business itself. Show the bridge: a backlog you ordered, a decision you made with data, a stakeholder you aligned. Certifications open the door to interviews; the stories with outcomes get the job.
points: PSPO I: Scrum.org assessment, online and timed, no mandatory course, does not expire.
Prepare with the Scrum Guide 2020, the EBM Guide and the open assessment.
CSPO (Scrum Alliance): earned by attending a course.
PO vs PM: often team and backlog vs market and strategy; check the job description.
Interviews: product sense, prioritisation, stakeholders, delivery; STAR stories with numbers.

example.code:
STAR story: saying no with data
Situation: Head of Sales asked for a custom quote builder for one big prospect.
Task:      Protect the Product Goal (payroll without an accountant) due in June.
Action:    Showed the cost (3 sprints, 6 weeks of delay for 2,400 shops),
           offered logo + colours on the existing quote in 2 days,
           put the full builder in NEXT with a trigger of 5 prospects.
Result:    Deal signed with the small version; Product Goal reached in June;
           shops running payroll alone went from 35 % to 58 %.
example.note: One story, four letters, one measured result: the format interviewers expect.

items: The long-term change the product brings to its users
For (customer) who (need), the (product) is a (category) that (benefit); unlike (alternative)…
Which segment, problem and business model first to move toward the vision
Future state of the product the Scrum Team plans against; one at a time
Roman Pichler’s one-page canvas: vision, target group, needs, product, business goals
Outputs with dates; promises what the team knows least
Results to reach and problems to solve; features are ideas
Horizons of growing uncertainty instead of dates
Group of work around a goal or customer problem
A change in customer behaviour or business result
Sorts stakeholders by power and interest into four strategies
Every new item delays everything below it
Accountable for maximizing the value of the product and for Product Backlog management
Decide how much work they take into the Sprint and how to do it
Accountable for the Scrum Team’s effectiveness; helps the PO with backlog techniques
Ongoing activity to detail, order and size items; not an event
Working session with stakeholders on progress toward the Product Goal; max 4 h for one-month Sprints
Only the Product Owner, when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete
Done work per Sprint; one team’s planning aid, never a target
Sprints needed: remaining points ÷ average velocity, rounded up
Optimistic with the highest velocity, pessimistic with the lowest
Chart of done work and total scope over time
Simulation from past throughput giving dates with probabilities
Adding people to a late project makes it later
Scrum.org framework to measure value with evidence
Value still possible: the gap customers still feel
How fast the organization delivers and learns
How well it can deliver new capabilities
Far, ambitious EBM goal; reached through Intermediate and Immediate Tactical Goals

pitfalls: A roadmap of features with dates months ahead, which turns every learning into a broken promise.
A vision that is a feature list, so nobody can use it to say no.
Saying yes to the loudest stakeholder without showing what moves down the backlog.
Requests reaching developers directly, bypassing the one Product Backlog.
Giving one release date instead of a range, and not updating it when the scope grows.
Using velocity as a target or comparing it between teams, which inflates the points.
Reporting outputs (features shipped) instead of outcomes and value.

exercises.q: In D2, the number of Sprints needed to finish the release (a Sprint cannot be split).
exercises.hint: Remaining points ÷ average velocity, rounded up with ROUNDUP(…, 0).
exercises.explain: 240 ÷ 34 = 7.06. ROUND would give 7 and leave 2 points undone; the release needs an 8th Sprint, so round up: 8.

exercises.q: In E2, the forecast as a range: optimistic Sprints (highest velocity) "to" pessimistic Sprints (lowest velocity), followed by " sprints", e.g. 5 to 8 sprints.
exercises.hint: Join two ROUNDUP results with & and the texts " to " and " sprints".
exercises.explain: 240 ÷ 42 = 5.71, so 6 Sprints at best; 240 ÷ 28 = 8.57, so 9 Sprints at worst: "6 to 9 sprints". The highest velocity gives the optimistic (smaller) number.

exercises.q: In E2, the number of weeks until the release, with Sprints of the length in D2 (in weeks).
exercises.hint: Whole Sprints first (ROUNDUP), then multiply by the Sprint length.
exercises.explain: ROUNDUP(240 ÷ 34) = 8 Sprints × 2 weeks = 16 weeks. Multiplying before rounding (240 ÷ 34 × 2 = 14.1) forgets that the last Sprint is a full Sprint. Add the weeks to the start date of the next Sprint for a date, and present it as the most likely point of a range.

exercises.q: Put the steps of building a roadmap in order.
steps: Start from the product vision and the current Product Goal
Gather evidence: customer problems, data, stakeholder input
Define the outcomes to reach and group them into themes
Place the themes in now, next and later
Review the draft with key stakeholders and agree the trade-offs
Share it and update it after each big learning or each quarter
exercises.answer: Vision → evidence → outcomes and themes → horizons → stakeholder review → share and update. A roadmap built from a list of requests skips the first three steps.

exercises.q: Sort these roadmap items into outputs and outcomes.

groups.name: Outcome
items: Halve the onboarding time of new teams
Raise the 90-day retention of small customers

exercises.answer: An output is something shipped; an outcome is a measurable change for customers or the business. An outcome roadmap lists the outcomes and keeps the outputs as ideas that can be replaced.

exercises.q: Match each stakeholder quadrant with its strategy.
pairs: Manage closely: involve them in decisions
Keep satisfied: short updates, no surprises
Keep informed: regular updates, ask for feedback
exercises.answer: The power / interest grid gives each group its own level of involvement. Redraw it when people or priorities change.

exercises.q: At a steering meeting, the CEO says: "I need a firm date for the new payroll release. Promise me 15 March." The team has 240 points left and a velocity between 28 and 42.

choices.label: Give the range: 6 to 9 Sprints, most likely 8, and what it means in dates
choices.feedback: A range with a most likely point is honest and still useful for planning.

choices.label: Promise 15 March to keep the CEO happy
choices.feedback: A promise with no basis becomes a broken promise, and the team pays for it with overtime or poor quality.

choices.label: Refuse to give any date: Scrum has no deadlines
choices.feedback: Scrum does not forbid forecasts. Refusing to answer loses the CEO’s trust.

steps.text: The CEO insists: 15 March is the date of a trade fair and cannot move. What do you propose?

choices.label: Fix the date and flex the scope: order the backlog so the most valuable part is ready by 15 March
choices.feedback: With a fixed date, scope is the variable. The CEO chooses what matters most for the fair.

choices.label: Add four developers from another team
choices.feedback: Late additions need onboarding and coordination; as Brooks’s law says, it often makes things later.

choices.label: Ask the Developers to commit to more points per Sprint
choices.feedback: Velocity is not a lever. Pushing it inflates points or cuts quality, and the Definition of Done suffers.

steps.text: How do you keep the CEO informed until March?

choices.label: A release burn-up updated every Sprint and shown at the Sprint Review, with early warning if the scope grows
choices.feedback: Transparency every Sprint: no surprise in March.

choices.label: A status mail the week before the fair
choices.feedback: Too late to change anything if the forecast has moved.

exercises.answer: Give a range, not a promise; with a fixed date, negotiate the scope; update the forecast every Sprint and show it openly.

exercises.q: According to the 2020 Scrum Guide, who decides how many Product Backlog items are selected for the Sprint?
exercises.answer: The Developers select how much they can do, after the PO explains the most important items and how they relate to the Product Goal. The PO orders the backlog; the Developers decide how much and how.

exercises.q: Which statement about the Product Owner matches the 2020 Scrum Guide?
options: The PO can be a committee of business representatives
The PO assigns Sprint Backlog items to Developers
The PO can delegate Product Backlog work but remains accountable
The PO must attend the Daily Scrum to collect status
exercises.answer: The Product Owner is one person, accountable for effective Product Backlog management even when others do part of the work. The Developers own the Sprint Backlog and the Daily Scrum.

exercises.q: The four Key Value Areas of Evidence-Based Management are Current Value, Unrealized Value, Time to Market and Ability to ___.
exercises.answer: Current Value, Unrealized Value, Time to Market and Ability to Innovate. Read them together: high Current Value with a low Ability to Innovate points to growing technical debt.

exercises.q: 210 points remain. The team’s velocity ranged from 25 to 35 over the last Sprints. Complete the forecast range.
exercises.answer: 210 ÷ 35 = 6 Sprints at best; 210 ÷ 25 = 8.4, rounded up to 9 Sprints at worst. Say "6 to 9 Sprints" and update it every Sprint.

exercises.q: Sales, support and management sent you this list: SSO login, invoice export to Excel, guided first payroll, dark mode, error checks before payroll submit, multi-site accounts, shift swap on mobile, custom quote builder. The Product Goal is "shops with up to 20 staff run payroll without an accountant". Turn the list into a now / next / later roadmap with outcomes.
exercises.answer: NOW, theme "Payroll without an accountant" (outcome: share of shops running payroll alone from 35 % to 60 %): guided first payroll, error checks before submit. NEXT, theme "Fewer support tickets and admin" (outcome: payroll tickets per 100 shops down): invoice export to Excel, SSO login if bigger customers confirm the need. LATER, problems worth solving: multi-site shops copying data by hand (multi-site accounts), staff who cannot swap shifts without calling (shift swap on mobile). Not on the roadmap for now: dark mode (no evidence of value) and the custom quote builder (one prospect; a smaller version or a trigger instead). Each horizon shows the outcome and the evidence; the features are current ideas, not dated promises, and the roadmap is reviewed with stakeholders.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Product Owner (1/6). You are the new PO of Coiflo, a fictional booking app sold by subscription to independent hair salons in France (1,800 paying salons). The CEO’s goal for the next two quarters: cut churn. Numbers: monthly churn 3.1 %; 64 % of appointments are booked online; 12 % of online appointments end in a no-show; in the exit survey of the last 6 months, 46 % of the salons that left named no-shows, 18 % the price, 9 % the lack of a multi-salon view; 7 % of accounts run more than one salon. Interview notes: (1) Owner, Lyon: “On Saturdays I lose 3 or 4 slots to no-shows, so I call every client the day before myself.” (2) Owner, Bordeaux: “Four no-shows last week. But a deposit would scare my older clients away.” (3) Manager of 2 salons, Lille: “I want one screen with both agendas; today I keep two tabs open.” (4) Hairdresser, Nantes: “Clients book a colour in a 30-minute slot, then I have to call them to move it.” (5) Owner, Paris: “Tourists ask for the booking page in English.” Which opportunity do you put in Now?
options: Lower the price so that salons stop leaving
exercises.hint: Which problem is backed by several sources at once: the exit survey, the interviews and the usage numbers?
exercises.answer: No-shows are the reason most often given by the salons that left (46 %), they come up in two interviews out of five and they touch the 64 % of appointments booked online: it is the problem with the most evidence and the closest link to the churn goal. Multi-salon matters to 7 % of accounts and 9 % of leavers: a real candidate for Later. The English page comes from one interview. A price cut is a business decision, not a product opportunity the team can test in a Sprint. Note 4 (a colour booked in a slot that is too short) is a second, smaller problem to keep in the backlog: a duration per service.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Product Owner (2/6). The team will work on no-shows. Write 3 to 5 user stories for the first release, each with 1 or 2 acceptance criteria in Given / When / Then. Keep note 2 in mind: some clients would not accept a deposit.
exercises.hint: Think of three moments: before the appointment (remind, confirm), when a client cancels (free the slot), after (see the effect). One story = one user, one need, one benefit.
exercises.answer:
Story 1: As a salon owner, I want my clients to get an automatic text message 24 hours before their appointment, so that I stop calling them one by one.
AC1: Given an appointment booked online for tomorrow at 10:00, When it is 10:00 today, Then the client receives a text with the date, the time, the salon and a link to confirm or cancel.
AC2: Given a salon that turned reminders off, When one of its appointments is due tomorrow, Then no text is sent.

Story 2: As a client, I want to confirm or cancel from the reminder in one tap, so that I do not have to phone the salon.
AC1: Given I open the link, When I tap “Cancel”, Then the appointment is cancelled, the slot is free again in the agenda and the salon sees the cancellation.
AC2: Given the appointment starts in less than 2 hours, When I open the link, Then I can no longer cancel online and I see the salon’s phone number.

Story 3: As a salon owner, I want to see which appointments are confirmed, so that I only call the clients who have not answered.
AC1: Given tomorrow’s agenda, When a client confirms, Then the appointment shows a “confirmed” mark.

Story 4: As a salon owner, I want to see my no-show rate per month, so that I know whether the reminders work.
AC1: Given appointments marked “no-show” by the salon, When I open the dashboard, Then I see the number and the rate of no-shows for each of the last 3 months.

Not in release 1: the deposit (note 2: test it later with volunteer salons) and the waitlist (it pays once cancellations arrive earlier). Each story is small enough for one Sprint, testable, and tied to the outcome: fewer no-shows.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Product Owner (3/6). The team estimated five candidate items (Reach = salons affected per quarter, Impact from 0.25 to 3, Confidence from 0 to 1, Effort in person-months). In F2, the RICE score of the first item, rounded to a whole number.
rows: Reminder text with confirm / cancel link
exercises.hint: RICE = Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort, all from row 2, inside ROUND(…, 0).
exercises.explain: 1,500 × 2 × 0.8 / 2.5 = 960. Copied down: waitlist 315, deposit 225, English page 75, multi-salon view 69 (69.33). The reminder comes first by far; the deposit has the biggest impact but its low confidence (note 2) and its effort pull it down: a small test can raise the confidence before anyone builds it. RICE ranks ideas, it does not decide alone (a strategic customer or a legal duty can change the order), so show the inputs next to the score.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Product Owner (4/6). Place these items on the roadmap. Team capacity: about 6 person-months a quarter. Goal: less churn through fewer no-shows.

groups.name: Now
items: Reminder text 24 hours before, with a confirm / cancel link
No-show rate on each salon’s dashboard

groups.name: Next
items: Waitlist that offers freed slots to other clients

exercises.hint: Now = the best score that serves the goal, plus how you will measure it; Next = what depends on Now or needs a test first; Later = real but smaller problems.
exercises.answer: Now attacks no-shows directly and measures the effect (2.5 person-months for the reminder plus a small dashboard: it fits the quarter with room for bugs). Next builds on Now: the waitlist only pays once cancellations arrive early, and the deposit is tested small because confidence is low. Later keeps real but smaller problems (7 % of accounts, one interview) with a trigger to bring them forward, for example a multi-salon chain ready to sign. Horizons, not dates.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Product Owner (5/6). The sales director writes: “A chain of 12 salons will sign if the multi-salon view is ready by 1 March. Put it in Now and give me a date.”

choices.label: Thank her, ask what the chain needs exactly and what the deal is worth, and explain the Now goal with its numbers
choices.feedback: You take the request seriously and get the facts (need, value, deadline) before any trade-off.

choices.label: Promise 1 March: a signature is a signature
choices.feedback: A date given before you know the scope and the cost becomes a broken promise, and the work on churn stops.

choices.label: Say no: multi-salon is in Later and the roadmap is decided
choices.feedback: A roadmap is a plan, not a contract. A flat no ignores new evidence and sends the conflict to the CEO without you.

steps.text: The chain needs to see the agendas of its 12 salons on one screen; read-only would do at first. What do you propose?

choices.label: A smaller version: a read-only combined view, estimated with the team, and what it would push out of Now
choices.feedback: Slicing the need often gives a cheap first step, and showing what moves out lets the decision rest on facts.

choices.label: Ask the team to squeeze it in without changing anything else
choices.feedback: Hidden extra work cuts quality, or the reminder release slips without anyone deciding it.

choices.label: Build the full multi-salon product to be safe
choices.feedback: A bigger scope means a later delivery, and still nothing for the chain by 1 March.

steps.text: The team estimates the read-only view at 1 person-month. The CEO asks for your view. What do you bring?

choices.label: The trade-off on one page: the deal’s value, the cost, what slips (the dashboard, by a few weeks) and your recommendation
choices.feedback: Clear options and a recommendation: the decision is made with you, in the open.

choices.label: Nothing: the PO decides alone what goes in the backlog
choices.feedback: The PO orders the backlog, but a trade-off about revenue and strategy is best made openly with the people accountable for it.

choices.label: Only the RICE table
choices.feedback: A score does not show the deal’s value, the deadline or what slips: tell the story around it.

exercises.answer: Listen and get the facts, slice the request, show its cost as what moves, recommend, and let the accountable person decide in the open. Then update the roadmap and tell sales what was decided and why. Never a date before you know the scope; when the date is fixed, the scope is the variable.

exercises.q: Take-home case, Product Owner (6/6). Write your recommendation to the CEO in 8 to 12 lines: the problem and its evidence, the outcome and how you will measure it, the Now / Next / Later roadmap, what you will not do and why, the risks, and when you will review it.
exercises.hint: Lead with the decision, then the evidence. Outcomes with a baseline and a target, not features with dates.
exercises.answer:
Recommendation: spend the next quarter on no-shows, the first reason why salons leave us.
Evidence: 46 % of the salons that left in the last 6 months named no-shows; 12 % of online appointments are missed; 2 of the 5 owners interviewed lose several slots a week and call clients by hand.
Outcome: no-shows on online appointments from 12 % to 8 % by the end of the quarter (target confirmed after 4 weeks of data), then monthly churn from 3.1 % towards 2.5 % over two quarters (churn moves slowly: we follow it every month).
Now: reminder text with confirm / cancel (RICE 960) and the no-show rate on each salon’s dashboard. Next: waitlist for freed slots (315), deposit test with 20 volunteer salons (225, low confidence). Later: multi-salon view (69; a read-only version for the 12-salon chain if the deal is confirmed) and the English booking page (75).
Not now: a price cut (a business decision, not a product bet) and a redesign of the agenda (no evidence of value).
Risks: each text message has a cost (to include in the plan or the subscription); some clients will ignore reminders; a deposit may upset older clients, hence a small test first.
Review: the no-show numbers at every Sprint Review, the roadmap with you and sales at the end of the quarter.

interview.q: What is the difference between a product vision, a product strategy and a Product Goal?
interview.a: The vision is the long-term change for users and stays stable for years. The strategy is how we move toward it: which segment, which problem, which business model first. The Product Goal, in the 2020 Scrum Guide, is the next future state of the product the Scrum Team plans against, one at a time, measurable in a few months. I would give the vision in one sentence, the current goal and the number that shows our progress.

interview.q: How do you build a roadmap, and why not a list of features with dates?
interview.a: I start from the vision and the Product Goal, gather evidence from customers, data and stakeholders, define outcomes and group them into themes, then place them in now, next and later. Feature dates months ahead promise what we know least and turn every learning into a broken promise. An outcome roadmap tells stakeholders what we will achieve and leaves the team free to find the best solution. I review it every quarter and after any big learning.

interview.q: Tell me about a time you said no to a senior stakeholder.
interview.a: I would use a STAR story: the request, what it would cost (the items it would delay), the data (how many customers, revenue at stake), the alternative I offered (a smaller version, a test, a place in Next with a trigger), and the result. The key points are understanding the need behind the request, making the trade-off visible, and telling the person the decision and the reason the same day so the relationship stays good.

interview.q: Two directors give you opposite priorities. What do you do?
interview.a: I put both requests in the one Product Backlog with the same data: the outcome they serve, reach, value and effort. Then I bring both directors together, show the trade-off and the link to the Product Goal, and make the ordering decision, which is the Product Owner’s accountability. If the conflict is about strategy rather than the backlog, I escalate to the product sponsor with the options. I write down the decision and the reasons.

interview.q: Management asks when the release will be ready. How do you answer?
interview.a: With a range from the team’s data: remaining points divided by the highest and lowest recent velocity, rounded up to whole Sprints, for example 6 to 9 Sprints, most likely 8. If the date is fixed, I order the backlog so the most valuable part comes first and the scope flexes. I show a release burn-up at every Sprint Review so a change in scope or pace is visible early. I never use velocity as a target or add people late.

interview.q: What does the Product Owner do in Sprint Planning and the Sprint Review?
interview.a: In Sprint Planning I bring an ordered Product Backlog and explain how the top items serve the Product Goal; the whole Scrum Team crafts the Sprint Goal and the Developers decide how much they take and how. In the Sprint Review the team presents the Increment to key stakeholders, we discuss progress toward the Product Goal and what changed in the market, and the Product Backlog is adjusted. It is a working session, not a demo.

interview.q: How do you measure whether your product delivers value?
interview.a: With outcomes, not outputs. I like Evidence-Based Management from Scrum.org: a few measures in each of the four Key Value Areas, Current Value, Unrealized Value, Time to Market and Ability to Innovate, tracked over time. Each roadmap outcome has its metric, and the trend tells me whether to continue, change or stop. Reading the four areas together shows trade-offs, such as revenue growing while technical debt slows innovation.

interview.q: What is the difference between a Product Owner and a Product Manager?
interview.a: It depends on the company. Often the Product Manager looks outward and further ahead (market, pricing, strategy, sometimes several teams) while the Product Owner is the Scrum accountability, working closely with one or two teams on the Product Backlog and value delivered each Sprint. In many companies one person does both. I would explain how I have covered both sides: discovery and strategy, and backlog and delivery.
